title: Chapter VIII

teacherSummary.text: Gatsby tells Nick of his love for Daisy in 1917. Nick tells him 'They're a rotten crowd.' Michaelis comforts Wilson, who believes God sees everything. Wilson tracks down Gatsby's house, shoots him in his pool, then kills himself.

context.history: Fitzgerald alternates Nick's account with the testimony of Michaelis, the Greek coffee-shop owner beside Wilson's garage, as at an inquest. Wilson's belief that the billboard eyes are God's draws on the period's loss of traditional faith that writers such as T. S. Eliot (The Waste Land, 1922) described.

significance: Gatsby dies waiting for a call that never comes, still loyal to Daisy; Wilson, misled by Tom, becomes the instrument of the rich couple's carelessness. Nick's compliment is the only judgment he speaks aloud to Gatsby.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter VIII,” how does Fitzgerald show Gatsby's death? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter VIII, how does Fitzgerald develop the idea of Gatsby's death? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter VIII develops the idea of Gatsby's death. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter VIII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Gatsby's death. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter VIII suggests about Gatsby's death. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and symbolism), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how F. Scott Fitzgerald uses characterization in Chapter VIII to complicate the reader's understanding of Gatsby's death. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter VIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of Gatsby's death responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter VIII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of Gatsby's death follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter VIII and its treatment of Gatsby's death. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and symbolism, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter VIII as evidence for a larger claim about Gatsby's death in The Great Gatsby. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter VIII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of Gatsby's death. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Great Gatsby.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: the green light
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The light at the end of Daisy's dock: Gatsby's dream, distant and unreachable, and finally the "orgiastic future" that recedes before everyone. In this chapter: “stood there for a minute and then turned out the light” (Chapter VIII, paragraph 3).

symbolsAndMotifs.name: eyes and seeing
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The billboard eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg, the owl-eyed man and Nick's watching: who sees, who judges, and whether anyone is watching at all. In this chapter: “men had already loved Daisy—it increased her value in his eyes. He felt their presence all about the house, pervading the air” (Chapter VIII, paragraph 10).

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Wilson shoots Gatsby and then himself. Use the safe-messaging script; discuss grief, misinformation and Tom's role, not methods.
contentNotes.studentPreview: This chapter includes a killing and a suicide. Support is available if this is hard to read.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “How did a lie lead to these deaths?”

safeMessaging.teacherScript: Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.
safeMessaging.studentResource: If you or someone you know is struggling or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, U.S.) or talk with a school counselor today.
safeMessaging.counselorPrompt: Let a counselor know in advance that this chapter is being taught.
